I hope this is the correct place to discuss the TPP in general.

I've been spending months advocating a “wait and see” approach to the TPP. I didn't think it was right to prejudge the treaty as a whole based solely on the leaks. However now that the treaty is ready and the text has been released, I'm not seeing any articles actually citing how it's bad. The caliber of evidence has not changed since the text was released even though every site voat is linking to seems to be saying “it's worse than we imagined”. However I didn't start on the free-trade agreement band wagon, I got here with evidence, and I would like to be able to leave with some.

For the sake of argument lets agree that “free trade” as in no taxes or restrictions on cross boarder goods or services is good. I don't feel like going back and forth debating what statisticians gleam out of decades of population data. I think this is fair because if you don't think this basic definition of free trade is good than you wouldn't like the TPP regardless of what's in it.

The big arguments I hear against are:

  • ISDS will let the treaty over-ride laws. It won't.
  • The treaty enacts some new terrible law. It doesn't.
  • ISDS will let the treaty over-ride laws. It won't.

For this I could be convinced with either:

A previous unfair ISDS ruling, that a company won, and the government changed it's laws. The exaggeration of ISDS was why I was against free-trade agreements before, and reading the supposed terrible rulings is what changed my mind. Link to an actual dispute, not just an article about them; I have to say this because I have seen a lot of baseless un-cited stuff surrounding this. An article that has an actual citation is fine, however I have seen some of these that take quite the artistic license with what the dispute was about. Changed it's law is important because there are some, like the USA lost an online casino one, that the USA just decided to let the island setup tariffs if they want because the USA wasn't going to allow online gambling. If the ISDS don't actually affect anything then I don't really see a problem with letting some lawyers yell at each other in a room.

Some evidence, as in a citing in the treaty, that ISDS are significantly different in the TPP. Up to about a ten page section, not “the whole intellectual property section” because that's hundreds of pages covering hundreds of things.

  • The treaty enacts some new terrible law. It doesn't.

For this I could be convinced with an example of a bad law that is in the treaty, but not already a law in the USA. For example there is a lot of noise about the ISP safe harbor provisions or not being allowed to unlock your phone, but those are both in the DMCA and I've lived under them for almost 20 years. I'm not saying the DMCA is a good law, just that it being in the TPP won't change anything, for me. It's the same with copyright extension, the fact that Malaysia will have to extend copyright to match the USA, not a big deal. Again cite up to about ten pages, I'm not reading the entire intellectual property chapter to try and find something someone else might think is bad.

Argument that doesn't matter: “We where not given a seat at the table” I just want to talk about this treaty we have now, not the entire process of how laws are made. Now that we have the treaty, I want to know why it's bad.

ISDS that are not settled so they don't count: Phillip Morris, that whole cigarette warning label thing in Australia; The Egyptian minimum wage increase, yea it was bad that they brought that up but it's undecided and three governments ago in Egypt. The Quebec fracking ban, I think this one might have merit but Quebec is just acting like it doesn't exist and has kept it's ban in place so no corporate over-ride.

ISDS short list that I think are reasonable but still open to my mind being changed: The Mexican toxic waste dump, The Peruvian Smelter, Dolphin safe tuna, The USA “country of origin label”
